text: Moa bones show just how violent that impact could be, and Maori legends describe
a giant eagle called the Poakai that swooped down and took children.
Imagine being told to get water from the river to make breakfast, and next
thing you know, you're some bird's curbside pickup for its three bratty kids.
Which brings us to the part where we make sure that doesn't happen to you.
Your entire strategy depends on one thing, seeing it before it sees you.
Scan the canopy constantly.
If it commits to the dive and you see it coming, throw yourself sideways at the
last second and get anything above your head.
A branch, a backpack, a random Maori kid, eh, nah, don't do that, a branch.
Just use a branch.
If it lands on you, grab both legs immediately.
It weighs 33 pounds, you do not.
Slam it a couple of times into the ground, and you should be fine.
Humans didn't hunt the eagles, but they hunted the moa, and the loss of
their primary food source drove the eagles to extinction.
Terror Bird
I want to start by addressing the name, because whoever came up with it clearly had no interest
in sugarcoating the situation for anyone.
The terror bird lived across South and North America, between 62 million and around 10,000
years ago.
Which means our ancestors shared the continent with this thing and decided to stay anyway.
